body_markdown:
You know someone really loves cars by the chances they take on them—not because they have to take those chances, but because they want to. (Let’s be honest, the lines blur.) Car people accept risks no sane person would because we know—or hope or dream—that in exchange we will get an experience we never would otherwise. We’ll learn new skills and meet new people, all while taking pride in owning something we truly care about, that reflects our personal tastes and/or history. Very likely, we will discover new parts of ourselves.


In that positive light, allow us to present what might have been our poorest automotive choices. They turned out pretty okay, if we say so ourselves, because they weren’t poor choices: They were gambles, and we went in with our eyes (mostly) open.


## Turning My Daily Driver Into My Race Car


My first award, a fourth-place at Mid-Ohio in 2007.


Eddy Eckart


When I was 25, in the winter of 2005, I did something really dumb. I used a home equity loan to turn my daily-driver Miata into a race car. I don’t recommend this to anyone, but the payoff has been immeasurable. It’s been the literal vehicle for countless memories, several of my closest friendships, landing my dream job here at Hagerty, and I still have it 21 years later. *— Eddy Eckart*


## Sight Unseen, on eBay: A Story in Two Parts


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


Max Berg


You win some, you lose some. I’ve twice bought vehicles, sight-unseen, on eBay. First came a 1971 VW T2 Westfalia camper, which gave the family[two years of happy holidays](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/a-tale-of-two-campers-shows-how-vw-vanlife-has-moved-upmarket/) before I sold it for a (small) profit. The second was the 1982 Lotus Esprit S3 that long-term readers[may remember](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/the-long-goodbye-to-my-lotus-esprit/) . It was bought in lockdown when, despite having plenty of time, I was too impatient to keep looking. Over the next four years, I went on to spend too much on sorting it out and sold it for too little. Will I be more cautious before my next roll of the dice on a classic? I hope so. *— Nik Berg*


## My First Porsche


[Nathan Petroelje](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nathan-petroelje/)


The first car that I paid for with my own money was a 1987 Porsche 924S. I was in college at the time. The car cost exactly all of my meager savings plus a little help from my grandmother. To tell you the truth, I didn’t even realize what a gamble that little car was at the time. I was just hyperfixated on the fact that I could say “Yeah, I own a Porsche,” which at the time was my favorite brand. I had no idea that on older cars like this, sometimes things just stop working and fixing them isn’t as simple as hopping down to a parts store.


For a surprising amount of time, my gamble paid off. Nothing major broke, and I got real joy out of driving it around campus. But the house always wins, and eventually the issues piled up to the point where I had to park the car for a prolonged period of time because I lacked time and money to make it right. We got it back on the road eventually, and I sold it and somehow came out only a few hundred dollars in the red. *— Nate Petroelje*


## A Facebook Marketplace XR600R


Kyle Smith


I don’t know if I would call many of my automotive adventures “gambling,” but that seems to stem more from the fact that I will overcalculate and cook the books until something I want to do no longer looks like it involves risk. At least that’s what it seems like because I bring home wrecks of projects with a glee reserved for a blackjack high roller arriving at their favorite casino.


Regardless, the biggest gamble I’ve taken in recent history was the 1988 Honda XR600R I found locally for sale and decided to[build it up to be the big-bore thumper of my dreams](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/reasons-excuses-and-the-big-dumb-bike-of-my-dreams/) . I figured I would replace so much of the chassis that the overall condition didn’t matter, so I didn’t inspect it much. This gamble did not pay when I opened the engine and found aluminum glitter and chunks sitting throughout.


I folded my cards and bought[a replacement engine that came in 14 boxes](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-honda-xr600r-project-is-going-to-hell-in-a-handbasket/) . Just because the last hand went poorly doesn’t mean the next will. *— Kyle Smith*


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


## A 13-Year-Old BMW Convertible


Eric Weiner


About 6 months into my professional car writing career, in 2014, I wasn’t making much money given my grim salary, rent, nights out with new friends in a new city, and so on. But I had some savings, garnered from years of jobs while in college, babysitting, and waiting tables in New York and Philadelphia. The sensible thing to do would have been to invest it. Instead, I spent more than half of my savings on a 13-year-old BMW convertible. That was a big risk—an American-built German car that was a decade out of warranty is never a cheap prospect—but I wasn’t even a year into my first gig in the industry. Would I flourish? Flame out? I didn’t know. I opted to feed my passion for cars and driving with the roadster I always wanted. It was a good call. Ann Arbor, where I live, is a college town, which means a lot of transient friendships. People spend a few years here, get their degree, and then move on. I had a lot of friend groups and changed apartments almost every year for a while. My Z3 was a constant, and has remained so. That buttoned-up straight-six and classic roadster proportions are as satisfying now as when I was single, new in town, and the greenest writer in the building. *— Eric Weiner*
